documentNotes.title: General note
documentNotes.statement: Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may have no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): **«situation is impossible – ситуация невозможна»**. Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

problems.title: Telescope.
problems.statement:
On the observational round you will use a simple Newton-system telescope with the mirror diameter $D=125$ mm, focal length $F=1025$ mm and 3 eye-pieces with focal lengths $f_1=12$ mm, $f_2=25$ mm and $f_3=38$ mm. Find on what distances ($\Delta x_1=$, $\Delta x_2=$, $\Delta x_3=$ in vertical direction on the middle figure) it is necessary to move the corresponding eye-pieces (1,2,3) to readjust the telescope from observation of the sky objects to observation of a monkey sitting at a distance $L=50$ m from you. (Your answer should have both formula and numerical values.) What eyepiece is the most suitable for observation of the monkey? Why?

![](p1-telescope)

solution.statement:
$$\frac1L+\frac1x=\frac1F,\qquad x=\frac{FL}{L-F}.$$

Sky objects: $L=\infty$, $x_0=F$.

Monkey: $L=L_m$, $x_m=FL_m/(L_m-F)$.

$$\Delta x_m=\Delta x_m-x_0=\frac{FL_m}{L_m-F}-F=\frac{F^2}{L_m-F}.$$

The answer does not depend on the focal lengths of the eye-piece, i.e.

$$\Delta x_1=\Delta x_2=\Delta x_3=\frac{F^2}{L_m-F}=\frac{1025^2}{50000-1025}=21.45\ \mathrm{mm}.$$

The eye-piece with the largest focal length is the most suitable for observation of the monkey. The magnification factors are $F/f$, for $f_1=12$ mm, $f_2=25$ mm and $f_3=38$ mm, which means that $\Gamma=85.4$, 41 and 26.9 respectively. So the effective distance of observing the monkey is $50\ \mathrm m/\Gamma$, 59 cm, 122 cm and 186 cm respectively. If you remember the field of view of any usual telescope and the size of a monkey, it would be evident that even for $f_3=38$ mm it is too difficult to observe the whole monkey to say nothing about $f_2=25$ mm and $f_1=12$ mm. So $f_3=38$ mm is the most suitable eye-piece among those that we have.

problems.title: False star.
problems.statement:
The White Bear (whom was already met in the VII, VIII, IX and X International Astronomy Olympiads) decided to connect a telescope to a film photo camera to make photos of constellations. The exposure times used were of order of 5 minutes. His comrade Penguin appears to be a great joker and bought a photoflash lamp. He decided to play a trick on the Bear and to “put” an extra star in his sky image, while the Bear photographed near-horizon constellations. The Penguin sitting in the photographic area of the Bear’s telescope (of course, relatively far from the telescope – 2.5 km) flashed once (sent one light pulse) to the camera during the exposure. Estimate the stellar magnitude of the false star in the Bear’s image.

Take into account the parameters of the flash pulse. The photographic conditions (sensitivity of film, diaphragm) while photographing objects with the flash at the distance of 1.5 metres (from both flash and camera) should be the same as while photographing the same objects on a sunny day with an exposure time of about 1/1000 second.

The solution has to include a picture with images of the telescope, Bear and Penguin.

solution.statement:
Let us compare light sources: the flash-lamp and the Sun. The fact, that the object’s illumination by the flash-lamp from a distance of 1.5 meters is the same as one by the Sun during 1/1000 seconds, show that the energies received by unit of the area of photographing are equal in these cases. That is, it is possible to make a conclusion about equivalence of one flash-pulse (it is not important, how long it lasts) from distance of 1.5 m and object $-26^m.8$ (stellar magnitude of the Sun), shining 1/1000 second.

But the Bear exposured the film during not 1/1000 second but 5 minutes = 300 seconds. During this time the same light energy on unit of the area will come from an object 300 000 times fainter than the Sun, that is, from object with 13.7 stellar magnitude larger, namely $-13^m.1$ or of order $-13^m$. For comparison – a little more bright than the full Moon.

The made conclusions concern to illumination by these objects of a photographed surface. But it is possible to make the same conclusions about the shining objects themselves being under photographing. Thus, for 300 seconds exposure the flash at the distance 1.5 m would look as object $-13^m.1$.

While increasing of the distance ($r$) to the flash the energy coming to a unit of area decreases as $1/r^2$. So increasing of the distance in 10 times leads to decreasing of light stream in 100 times ($5^m$ increasing of stellar magnitude), increasing of the distance in $2500/1{,}5\approx1670$ times – in 2 800 000 times. Accordingly, “the effective stellar magnitude of the flash” will increase on 16.1 and will make $3^m.0$. That is the Bear will find out “new object” of order $3^m$ at the sky image.

problems.title: Polar day and night.
problems.statement: Find the boundaries of the region of the polar day and the region of polar night at the dates when the Sun may be in Zenith in Mumbai, HBCSE. The latitude and longitude of HBCSE are $\lambda_C=72^\circ56'$, $\varphi_C=19^\circ03'$. Take as many effects as possible into account.

solution.statement: If the Sun is in zenith in any point, its declination is equal to the latitude of this point. Therefore those dates when the Sun can be in Bombay (HBCSE) in zenith, declination of the Sun is equal to $\delta=\varphi_C=19^\circ03'$. In this case (firstly refraction not taken into account) the center of the Sun during the current day never be under the horizon at northern latitudes above $(90^\circ-\delta)=(90^\circ-\varphi_C)$ and also never be above the horizon at latitudes to the south from $(-90^\circ+\delta)=(-90^\circ+\varphi_C)$. Taking into account refraction ($35'$ at horizon) and radius of the Sun ($16'$), it is possible to receive, that the top edge of the Sun during the current day never set under the horizon at northern latitudes above $(90^\circ-\varphi_C-51')$ and also never rise from the horizon at latitudes to the south from $(-90^\circ+\varphi_C-51')$. These latitudes are the real boundaries of polar day and polar night. For HBCSE $\varphi_C=19^\circ03'$ and the boundaries appear on $71^\circ06'$ N (polar day) and $72^\circ48'$ S (polar night).

problems.title: Galaxy.
problems.statement:
Figure 4.1. shows the distribution of hydrogen gas in the disk of the spiral galaxy NGC 1325 as a contour map. The contour image is superimposed on an optical image of the galaxy. Assume the disk of the galaxy to be nearly circular. Find the angular diameter of the galaxy. (As the angular size of the galaxy is small to an observer on the Earth, you can use plane geometry as an approximation.) Estimate the diameter and distance to the galaxy in kpc. Find the angle of inclination of the galaxy plane with respect to the plane of the sky.

![](p4-galaxy-map)

![](p4-optical-map)

solution.statement:
On the horizontal axis scale,

$$20\ \mathrm s=300''\text{ in R.A.}=300''\times\cos(21^\circ33')=279''\sim43.5\ \mathrm{mm}.$$

On the vertical axis scale,

$$5'=300''\sim46.7\ \mathrm{mm}.$$

Drawing the right angle triangle with the galaxy being hypotenuse, two sides are $47\ \mathrm{mm}\sim301''$ and $37\ \mathrm{mm}\sim238''$.

Thus, by Pythagoras theorem, the angular diameter of the galaxy is $384''\sim6'.5$.

From the length scale drawn on the right hand top corner, $5\ \mathrm{kpc}\sim7\ \mathrm{mm}\sim45''$.

Physical diameter of the galaxy $=5\times384/45=43$ kpc.

$$384''=1.89\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}.$$

Distance to the galaxy $=43\ \mathrm{kpc}/1.86\cdot10^{-3}=23$ Mpc.

We may find this distance also directly from the scale $5\ \mathrm{kpc}=45''$, so the distance to the galaxy $=206265\times5\ \mathrm{kpc}/45=23$ Mpc.

Using a simple metre scale, in the first figure, the axes of the ellipse can be measured: $b=20$ mm, $a=60$ mm.

Thus, $i=\cos^{-1}(b/a)=\cos^{-1}(20/60)=\cos^{-1}(0.33)\approx70^\circ$.

**Note:** From literature, $i=71^\circ$.

problems.title: Lunar satellite.
problems.statement:
These are two photos of the Moon taken by the same camera mounted on a lunar satellite. The first photo has been made while the satellite was near its periselenion and the second one near the aposelenion. Find from these data the value of the satellite’s orbit eccentricity. Estimate the minimum period between the moments at which these two photos could be taken.

![](p5-moon-pair)

solution.statement:
The hemisphere of the Moon at photos is about the same as we see it from the Earth.

Taking into account that the Moon is faced to us by one side all the times, it is possible to draw a conclusion that photographing was made from the points of space located approximately between the Earth and the Moon.

The Moon’s image diameter ($d$) at every photo is proportional to its angular size visible from the satellite: $d\sim\alpha=D/L$, where $D$ – real diameter of Moon and $L$ – the distance to it. $D$ is constant and $L$ is depend on position of the satellite:

$L=L_0(1+e)$ for aposelenion;

$L=L_0(1-e)$ for periselenion.

So if we have diameters of Moon’s image at periselenion ($d_P$) and aposelenion ($d_A$) of the satellite’s orbit we may write:

$$d_P/d_A=\alpha_P/\alpha_A=[D/(1-e)]/[D/(1+e)]=(1+e)/(1-e).$$

And: $e=(1-d_P/d_A)/(1+d_P/d_A)$.

The presented two pictures have been taken for moments near periselenion and aposelenion (not just at periselenion and aposelenion), so $d_1\approx d_P$ and $d_2\approx d_A$; instead of “=” in the previous formula we should write “$\approx$”:

$$e\approx(d_1-d_2)/(d_1+d_2).$$

By measuring the images one may found $d_1\approx46.5$ mm, $d_2\approx40.5$ mm.

$$e\approx(d_1-d_2)/(d_1+d_2)\approx0.07.$$

Taking into account the satellite’s orbit is more or less stable in the space, it will take about half a year to change the situation “full Moon at periselenion” to “full Moon at aposelenion” (the Sun to be at the opposite direction from the Moon).
